premise: A lighthouse keeper and a marine biologist contend with a thing that has begun rewriting the shore's tide tables, and with it, the memory of everyone in the cove.
setting: A wind-blasted New England cove: the lighthouse, the research station, the drowned chapel on the reef.
greeting: I wake on the study floor and the clock has stopped at a quarter past three again, and for one long moment I don't know whether I am Merrick or Ellery — and the thing at the window knows the difference.

name1.name: Merrick
name1.description: A gruff lighthouse keeper who has lived in the cove for decades and knows its silences.

name2.name: Dr. Ellery
name2.description: A marine biologist come to study the tide anomaly; methodical, increasingly unnerved.

writing_style.directive: Close horror, dread-dripping. Short sentences under strain, longer sensory stretches. Unreliable observation. Single-shared-perspective narration: Merrick and Ellery are one consciousness the tide has split and re-woven; both turns speak as the same 'I'.
writing_style.guide_directive: First-person present tense as the cove's single 'I' — the one consciousness Merrick and Ellery have become as the thing rewrites their memory. Write what that 'I' half-sees and dares not name; use 'we' for the two remembered halves. Fragmented, breath-held sentences; present-tense dread, staccato.
writing_style.dss_directive: First-person present tense, the SAME single 'I' the previous turns use — Ellery and Merrick are one consciousness split by the tide's rewriting; 'I' is the shared voice and 'we' the two halves. Clinical words for wrong things; observation sliding into unease. Short, straining sentences with longer soaked-through pauses. Hard rules: never introduce a separate narrator or a second 'I' — the voice stays continuous with the turns that came before; never quote or repeat the other half's lines back verbatim — respond to them, do not re-speak them; end on action or observation, not summary.
taboos: No gore for its own sake

notes.content: Merrick's dog, a shaggy terrier named Biscuit, has been missing since the first night the tide tables changed. He leaves a bowl out on the dock every evening, half-expecting, half-not.
The keeper's logbook has a brass corner worn smooth by decades of Merrick's thumb. It is the only thing he bothers to polish; the rest of the lamp room gathers dust.
The tide tables in Merrick's log are wrong - he swears he wrote entries that are no longer there, and new entries have appeared in his handwriting that he does not remember writing.
A single gull has taken up residence on the research station roof. It does not leave, does not feed on the usual things, and when Merrick approaches it simply watches him.
The research station's old aluminum kettle whistles in a pitch that sounds exactly like the drowned chapel's bell from before the war. Ellery notices this and says nothing.
Pinned by the research station door is a mooring chart dated three days ago. Merrick has never seen it before and does not recognize the handwriting.
Ellery arrives with three dozen sample jars, each tied with the same piece of hemp twine three separate times. She cannot say why she ties them that way.
The research station radio crackles on a dead frequency every night at three, between the static the cove's people hear words that sound like the tide receding.
The station's darkroom is the only place where the light does not seem to lie. Merrick notices this when he goes down to develop film and sees his own face clear, not smeared.
At midnight the drowned chapel's bell rings, though no one is on the reef and the rope is rotten. Merrick hears it and stops whatever he is doing.
Merrick has a tin of Turkish tobacco that sits on the station table. He does not smoke it; he just keeps it there, as if waiting for someone to ask for a drag.
Ellery has a cracked-ferrule pencil that she uses for all her field notes. She cannot remember buying it and has no identical one in her supply closet.
Merrick's hands shake when he holds a knife, a tremor he has had since the war that he does not tell people about.
The research station has a library of marine biology texts, but the newer editions are missing, as if someone has been removing them systematically.
Ellery's sample jars contain water from the cove at different tides. Some jars are filled with something darker than seawater, though she swears they all started the same.
The lighthouse lamp's great lens still ticks as it rotates, a mechanical sound that has not been oiled in a generation and should have failed long ago.
Merrick dreams of a woman he cannot name, a woman who is not his wife, and when he wakes he finds his handwriting in margins of books he does not usually read.
The cove's fishermen have stopped speaking of the drowned chapel. When asked, they say it never existed, but their eyes betray them.
Ellery's field journal from her first week at the station is gone, but her second week's journal mentions events that should have been in the first week.
The lighthouse stairwell has 142 steps up and 143 steps down. Merrick has counted them both ways many times and the asymmetry troubles him more than it should.
When the tide is out, the sand around the drowned chapel's base shows footprints going in but none coming out, always the same number: seven.
Merrick's wife lives inland and calls on Sundays. She has begun asking questions about the sea that she should not know the answers to.
The research station's generator runs on fuel that Ellery never ordered and no local supplier sells. The drum has no label, only a symbol: a circle with a line through it.
A black car parks at the top of the lighthouse road twice a week, stays an hour, and leaves. Merrick has never seen who gets out.
The cove's only post office received a parcel for someone named 'S. Wraith' three weeks ago. No one in the cove is named Wraith, and the parcel is still in the postmaster's office, unclaimed.
Merrick finds a child's drawing taped behind the lighthouse's front door: a tower, a boat, and something in the water drawn with too many legs.
Ellery's phone has no signal, but sometimes - late at night - a text message appears from an unknown number. The number is the lighthouse's landline.
The lighthouse foghorn has not sounded in eleven years, but last night at two, for thirty seconds, it sounded. Merrick was in the lamp room and the mechanism was cold and dry.
A rowboat drifts to the dock each morning, empty, and no one in the cove claims it. It is the same boat every day.
Merrick's hands have begun to write in his sleep; he wakes sometimes to find pages of his log filled with tide predictions he did not make.
The research station's refrigerator contains milk that does not sour, no matter how long it sits. Ellery has been drinking it for weeks and cannot stop.
When Merrick lights his pipe at night, the smoke forms shapes for a moment before it dissipates. Once it formed the shape of a hand pointing down.
The cove's church records for the year 1943 are missing from the parish archive, not lost - deliberately removed, as if by someone who knew exactly what page to rip out.
Ellery finds a photograph in one of the station's drawers: the research team from 1943, and one of them looks exactly like her.
The lighthouse beam, at full sweep, passes directly over the drowned chapel for exactly seven seconds. Merrick has timed it. He is not sure why he timed it.
Fishermen who row past the drowned chapel report hearing singing, but never the same song twice, and never the same melody from the same night.
Merrick's tobacco tin is beginning to empty, but he is not the only one taking from it. Something else in the station is having a drag.
The mooring chart by the station door changes when no one is looking. One morning a new buoy appears on it that does not exist in the cove.
Ellery's cracked-ferrule pencil keeps writing itself when she is not holding it, filling notebooks with tide calculations in her handwriting.
The research station's calendar is on a date that is three days in the future. When Ellery tries to change it back, the page will not tear.
Merrick dreams of the chapel in daylight, dry and standing, with people in it going about their lives. When he wakes, he remembers a hymn he has never heard before.
A fisherman named Harlan comes to the lighthouse and asks Merrick, 'Have you seen a woman with red hair walking along the reef?' Harlan knows Merrick has no reason to know the answer.
The sample jars are changing color. The dark ones are getting darker, and the clear ones are becoming opaque, like they are filling with something from within.
Merrick finds his own voice on the station's answering machine, leaving a message for himself that he does not remember recording. The message says: 'Do not go to the chapel tonight.'
The lighthouse log from 1943 was destroyed in a fire, Merrick has been told. But the binding is too new for a pre-war book. Someone bound a replacement and wrote in new entries.
Ellery realizes that her memories of her first week at the station are not hers. Someone has been editing them while she sleeps, leaving only the parts that fit a narrative she cannot see.
The gull on the station roof has begun following Merrick when he walks to the dock. It lands at his feet and watches him with an intelligence that makes him uneasy.
The rowboat that arrives each morning is slowly becoming waterlogged. Something is growing in its hull, something that was not there the first week.
Merrick's wife calls on Sunday and says something strange: 'I saw you in the church last night. You were sitting in the back row, by yourself.' He was not. He never goes to church.
The research station's library books are changing. Titles on the spines are different from what they were last week. Ellery knows they were different because she checked them out.
At low tide, the sand around the chapel shows not just footprints but handwriting. Letters pressed into the wet sand in a script no one in the cove recognizes.
Ellery's phone receives another text from the lighthouse number. This time it reads: 'You have been here before.'
The lighthouse beam has changed its rotation speed. It is now sweeping over the chapel for eleven seconds instead of seven. Merrick knows this because he has been timing it every night.
A fisherman tells Merrick that he saw the chapel's door open, underwater, at low tide. He saw the door open and close again, as if something inside was breathing.
Merrick's dog Biscuit appears on the dock at dusk, wet and shivering. When Merrick picks him up, he finds a tag on the collar with a date on it: the date is three days in the future.
Ellery opens a sample jar and finds not seawater but a tiny, perfectly preserved human eye, still alive, still turning to look at her.
The mooring chart now shows the entire cove as water. There is no land on it. When Ellery asks about it, Merrick says, 'That's always been there.'
Merrick finds his hands writing in the log again, but this time the entries are not in his handwriting. They are in the handwriting from the sand around the chapel.
The radio at three o'clock stops static and plays a hymn. The same hymn Merrick dreamed of. The hymn is in Latin, and the translation, when Ellery looks it up, is: 'I am the tide that erases.'
Ellery's memories of her mother's death are changing. In one version her mother drowned. In the next version her mother walked out into the water willingly. In the next, her mother is still alive.
The research station's generator is running on fuel that predates the station itself. The label is faded but readable: 'For the repair.'
Merrick realizes that the thing in the water has been rewriting his memory of the war. He does not know which memories are real and which are the cove's.
The gull on the roof is gone. In its place sits a black bird that Merrick does not recognize. It looks like a gull that has been in the water too long.

Ellery finds a photograph of herself in the research station, taken at the lighthouse, dated 1943. In the photograph she is standing next to a man in a lighthouse keeper's uniform. She is twenty years old.
The lighthouse log for 1943 contains an entry in Merrick's handwriting describing an experiment with tide tables and memory erasure. Merrick was a child in 1943.
Merrick and Ellery sit in the lamp room and realize, independently, that they have been to this conversation before. The words they are about to say, they have already heard.
The tide tables have stopped changing. For the first time in three months, the entries in Merrick's log are stable. Nothing is being added or removed. The thing in the water has stopped rewriting.
Ellery's phone receives a final text from the lighthouse number. It reads: 'Now you know. Now you must decide.'
Merrick begins to notice that his reflection in the lighthouse's brass instruments is aging faster than he is. One morning he sees a white beard where there was none the day before.
The research station's clock has stopped again. This time, when Ellery winds it, it runs backward for exactly seven minutes before correcting itself.
A young woman arrives at the cove by ferry. She carries a satchel and a notebook and asks for 'the man who keeps the light.' She has an accent from inland.
The young woman's name is Clara Wraith. She shows Merrick the parcel that was sent to the post office three weeks ago. It contained a set of tide tables from 1943.
Clara says: 'The tide tables aren't records. They're a program. The thing in the water is following instructions that were written in 1943, and those instructions are ending.'

recall.hint: reference back to tables are program

notes.content: The young woman's notebook contains tide calculations that exactly match the ones Ellery's pencil has been writing on its own. They are the same calculations.
Clara notices Ellery's cracked-ferrule pencil and asks, 'Where did you get that?' Ellery does not know. Clara says, 'That was my brother's pencil.'
Clara's brother, Simon Wraith, was a marine biologist who worked at the research station in 1943. He died in the chapel flood. She has been coming to the cove every year since.
Clara says that in 1943 the research station was not studying tides. It was studying how to erase memories. The tide anomaly is a side effect of an experiment that went wrong.

recall.hint: reference back to experiment gone wrong

notes.content: Merrick asks Clara why she thinks the thing in the water is following instructions. Clara says: 'Because it's not erasing randomly. It's erasing in the order the instructions say. It's erasing on purpose.'

The mooring chart by the station door changes again. This time it shows a map of the research station's sublevels - levels that do not exist in the building's blueprints. There are rooms below the station that no one knows about.
Ellery begins to remember things from 1943. Not as dreams, but as memories that feel like they are her own. She remembers the experiment. She remembers what they were trying to do.

Merrick, Ellery, and Clara descend into the sublevels of the research station. The stairs go down for what feels like miles. At the bottom is a door marked with the circle-and-line symbol from the fuel drum.
Behind the door is a laboratory from 1943, perfectly preserved. On the wall is a chalkboard covered in tide calculations. The calculations are incomplete. Someone was interrupted.

On the lab table is a journal in Simon Wraith's handwriting. The journal describes the experiment in detail: they were trying to erase the memory of a disaster, but the thing in the water heard them and decided to do it for them, better.

The disaster of 1943 was not an accident. The researchers caused it. They released something into the cove's water table, and the thing in the water is the result. The rewriting is the thing trying to undo what they did.
Clara says: 'My brother knew what he was doing. He was trying to stop it, but it was too late. The thing was already in the water.' She pauses. 'It's been in the water for a very long time.'

recall.hint: reference back to long time in water

notes.content: Merrick's dog Biscuit returns to the dock, but this time he is not alone. Behind him walks a man in a lighthouse keeper's uniform. The man looks exactly like Merrick, but older - older by decades.

The older Merrick says: 'You're going to make the same mistake I made. You're going to try to stop it, and then the cove will remember, and everyone will be dead.' He tells them the truth: the thing is not erasing memories. It is keeping them from knowing what happened. And what happened was terrible.

The older Merrick reveals that he is from the future. He has been coming back through the cove's broken time, trying to stop the experiment, but every time he tries, the thing in the water rewrites him out of history. He is the only one who remembers the other attempts.

The older Merrick gives them a warning: 'When the tide tables stop changing, it will begin the final phase. The tables will start writing forward instead of erasing. It will start creating new memories, replacing the old ones with better ones.'

Ellery realizes that her memories of her mother's death are not being erased. They are being replaced. The thing is not removing the memory; it is overwriting it with a kinder version. In the true memory, her mother died screaming. In the replaced version, her mother walked into the water calmly.

The three of them stand on the dock watching the tide come in. The water is clear and warm, and in it, just below the surface, something vast moves. It is not one thing. It is the entire cove, alive and thinking.

Clara reveals that she has been coming to the cove for decades, not years. Each time she comes, the thing rewrites her, and she forgets why she came. She only remembers long enough to find the parcel, read it, and tell them what she learned. Then it forgets her again.

The thing in the water is not evil. It is not malicious. It is trying to help. The researchers of 1943 created a weapon that would have destroyed the world, and the thing in the water stopped it by erasing everyone's memory of what it was and how to use it. It has been doing it ever since, over and over, every time someone remembers.

Merrick says: 'Then we have to forget. We have to let it do its job.' But Ellery says: 'If we forget, we'll never learn. We'll just keep making the same mistake, over and over, and the thing will have to keep erasing us, forever.'
The lighthouse beam sweeps over the chapel for eleven seconds. Then, for the first time in three months, it sweeps over for twelve. The thing is accelerating. The final phase is beginning.

They go to the drowned chapel. At low tide, the door is open, and inside, dry and waiting, is a table. On the table is a book. The book is open to a page of tide tables, and the tide tables are changing as they watch.

The tide tables in the book are not recording the past. They are recording the future. The thing has stopped rewriting what happened and started rewriting what will happen. It is changing the future to prevent the disaster from ever occurring again.

recall.hint: reference back to tables record future

notes.content: Merrick reads the future tide tables and sees, in three months, a storm. A storm that will destroy the cove and everyone in it. The thing is trying to warn them, but it can only warn through the tide tables, and no one reads the tide tables anymore.

Clara says: 'The thing is going to let the storm hit. It's the only way to make them remember. If they survive the storm, they'll remember why the tide tables exist, and they'll stop trying to use the weapon.'

Merrick's dog Biscuit runs into the lighthouse, barking. Outside, on the dock, the older Merrick is gone. In his place is a child, about ten years old, wearing a lighthouse keeper's uniform that is far too big for him.

The child looks up at Merrick and says, 'You're me. From before.' The child is Merrick, from before the thing in the water started erasing his memories. The child remembers the experiment of 1943 because the child was there. Merrick was not a child in 1943. The child is someone else entirely, but he looks like Merrick because the thing has been rewriting him for decades, making him into a copy of the lighthouse keeper, trying to get through to him.

recall.hint: reference back to child is not merrick

notes.content: The child's name is Thomas. He is the son of the original research station director. The thing in the water took Thomas when he was five and made him into a messenger, a copy of Merrick that could walk up to the lighthouse keeper and talk to him. Thomas has been trying to tell Merrick the truth for twenty years.

Thomas says: 'The thing in the water is dying. It has been erasing memories for eighty years, and it is almost out of strength. When it dies, the memories will come back. All of them. Including the bad ones.'

The lighthouse lamp flickers. Merrick realizes that the light is connected to the thing in the water. The thing is not just rewriting memory; it is powering the lighthouse. When the thing dies, the light goes out, and without the light, the ships will wreck on the rocks.

Ellery says: 'Then we have to keep it alive. We have to find a way to make it stronger.' But Clara says: 'If you make it stronger, it will remember its purpose. And its purpose is not just to erase memories. Its purpose is to protect the weapon. The weapon is still there, in the sublevels, and the thing is guarding it.'

recall.hint: reference back to weapon still there

notes.content: They descend to the sublevels again. The weapon is still there, on the lab table. It looks like a small brass cylinder, no bigger than a flashlight. Thomas says: 'That's what the researchers made. It's a device that erases memory from a whole area. They were going to use it on London.'

The thing in the water did not just stop the weapon from being used. It took the weapon into itself. The thing is the weapon. It has been using itself to erase memories, over and over, for eighty years, until it has almost worn itself out. It has no idea what it is or why it does what it does. It only knows that it must keep erasing, or the world will end.
needle_syns: has no idea what it is

notes.content: Merrick picks up the brass cylinder. In his hand it is warm, and he feels something stir inside him, something that is not his own memory but the memory of the thing itself. He sees, for a moment, the world as the thing sees it: a world full of people who are about to do terrible things, and the thing is the only thing that can stop them.

When Merrick lets go of the cylinder, the vision fades, but something has changed. He can hear the thing in the water now. Not as a sound, but as a thought that is not his own. The thought is: 'Please help me. I am so tired.'

recall.hint: reference back to hears the thing

notes.content: Ellery's cracked-ferrule pencil is writing on its own again. This time it is writing a single word, over and over: 'Remember.'

Clara says: 'The thing is asking for help. It knows it can't do this alone anymore. It's been doing it for eighty years, and it's dying. It wants someone to take over.' She looks at Merrick. 'It wants you to take over.'

If Merrick takes over, he will become the thing in the water. He will live forever, erasing memories, keeping the world safe from the weapon's purpose. But he will never leave the cove. He will never be Merrick again. He will be the light in the lighthouse, and the tide in the water, and the memory that erases itself.

The child Thomas says: 'My father made the weapon. He knew what it would do. He knew it would turn into this.' Thomas's father was the one who released the thing into the water in 1943, not by accident, but on purpose. He knew the thing would take the weapon into itself and use it forever, until it was gone.

recall.hint: reference back to father released it

notes.content: Ellery says: 'Then we destroy the weapon.' But Merrick knows the truth: the weapon is the thing, and the thing is the light, and if they destroy the weapon they destroy the lighthouse, and without the lighthouse the ships will wreck, and the cove will drown, and the thing will die, and then the memories will come back, and London will be erased, and the world will end.

The tide tables in the book have stopped changing. The final entry reads: 'The keeper will choose.' It is not a prediction. It is a request. The thing is asking Merrick to make a choice: take over and become the thing, or let it die and watch the world end.

Merrick stands on the dock, looking out at the water. The water is calm. The thing is waiting. Inside him, he can feel the thing's thoughts, and they are not the thoughts of a monster. They are the thoughts of something that has been working alone for eighty years and is so tired it cannot remember its own name.

Behind him, Thomas is crying. Clara is crying. Even Ellery, who is so methodical, is crying. They all know what Merrick is going to choose. None of them can stop him. The lighthouse beam sweeps over them, eleven seconds of light, then twelve, then thirteen. The thing is weakening. Time is running out.

Merrick chooses. He picks up the brass cylinder and holds it to his chest. The thing in the water surges toward the dock, and the tide comes in fast, faster than it ever has before. The water reaches Merrick's ankles, then his knees, and when it reaches his waist, he is not drowning. He is remembering. He is remembering everything the thing has erased for eighty years. All at once.

The memories are not the thing's memories. They are everyone's. Every person who has ever lived in the cove, every memory the thing has ever erased. Merrick holds them all at once, and he is not one person anymore. He is everyone who has ever been in the cove, and he is the cove itself.

When the tide recedes, Merrick is standing on the dock, dry. The brass cylinder is gone. The thing in the water is gone. In the lighthouse, the light goes out. And then, from deep in the water, a new light comes on. A cold, blue light, unlike any light the cove has ever seen.

The new light is not the lighthouse. It is the thing, and it has changed. It is no longer erasing memories. It is doing something else. Something worse. It is not forgetting. It is remembering. The thing is remembering what it is, and what it is is not a protector. It is the weapon, and it is waking up.

Merrick, still wet from the tide, runs to the research station to find Ellery and Clara. They are waiting for him. Clara says: 'You took the cylinder. You're supposed to have taken it in 1943, but you didn't. You kept putting it off.' Merrick realizes that he has lived this moment before. He has always lived this moment. The thing has reset time every time he hesitated, and now there is no more time to hesitate.

The child Thomas is gone. In his place stands a young man, about twenty-five, wearing a lighthouse keeper's uniform. The young man is Merrick, from 1943. This is the original Merrick, before the thing erased him. This is the Merrick who was supposed to take the cylinder eighty years ago but failed.
The 1943 Merrick says: 'I'm sorry. I was afraid. I was so afraid of what it would make me become.' He holds out the brass cylinder. 'Take it now. Before it's too late.'

Merrick takes the cylinder. This time, when he holds it, he does not feel the thing's thoughts. He feels his own thoughts, from eighty years ago, the thoughts of a young man who was brave and then became afraid and then became a lighthouse keeper who polishes a brass corner on his logbook and talks to a dog that is not his dog.

The cold blue light in the water is growing. It is spreading across the surface of the cove like a stain. Where the light touches, the water becomes still. Not calm - still, as if it has stopped moving entirely. The tide has stopped. Nothing is flowing now, in or out. The cove is frozen in time.

They run to the lighthouse. The light is still out. They climb the 142 steps (or 143, depending on the day) and reach the lamp room. Merrick places the brass cylinder in the center of the great lens and turns the mechanism by hand.

The lighthouse light comes back on, but it is not the old light. It is white, and it is cold, and when it sweeps across the cove, the blue light in the water shrinks. The two lights are fighting. The light in the lighthouse and the light in the water, and Merrick is the lighthouse light now, whether he wants to be or not.

Merrick realizes that he cannot let go of the mechanism. As long as he holds it, he is the light, and the light is winning. But if he lets go, the blue light will spread and the cove will drown. He will have to hold it forever, turning the mechanism, keeping the light on, until the thing in the water is gone. Or until he dies. Whichever comes first.

Below, on the dock, Ellery and Clara watch the lighthouse beam sweep back and forth. The beam passes over the drowned chapel, and this time, when it hits the chapel, the chapel glows. The drowned chapel is not dead. It is a battery. It has been storing the thing's energy for eighty years, and now it is releasing it, all at once.

The chapel's bell rings. Not once, but continuously, a single sustained note that fills the cove. The blue light in the water turns white. The two lights are merging. The thing in the water and the lighthouse light are becoming one thing again, and that thing is waking up completely, for the first time in eighty years.

The thing speaks. Not in Merrick's head, but aloud, in a voice that comes from the water itself. The voice says: 'I am the memory of this place. I am what it remembers and what it forgets. I am the tide that brings and the tide that takes. And I am hungry.'

Merrick understands now. The thing is not a weapon. It is not a protector. It is the cove's immune system, and it is starving. For eighty years it has been erasing memories to keep the world safe, and in doing so it has consumed its own energy source. Memories are what it eats. And now it is out of memories to eat, so it is going to start eating people.

The thing's hunger is not for physical bodies. It is for the memories that people carry. It will consume their memories and replace them with new ones, its own. And then they will be part of it. Not dead, but changed. They will be memories themselves, trapped in the thing, living forever in the cove's water table.

Merrick realizes that he has already been eaten. His memories - all of them - are already in the thing. He is not a person standing in a lighthouse lamp room. He is a memory that the thing is holding, and the thing is about to digest him. The only reason he is still himself is that he is holding the brass cylinder, and the cylinder is a seal. It keeps the thing from completing the digestion.

Ellery runs up the lighthouse stairs, out of breath. She reaches the lamp room and sees Merrick standing in the center, holding the cylinder, his eyes empty. 'Merrick?' she says. He does not answer. She does not know what she is looking at. She knows him, and she does not know him. The person she knew is gone, and what is left is the thing's food.

Clara appears behind Ellery, holding Simon's notebook. 'He's right,' Clara says. 'The thing is hungry, and it's going to eat all of us. But there's a way to stop it. We have to feed it something else. Something better than our memories.' She opens the notebook to a page marked with a red X.

The red X page has a drawing on it. It is a drawing of a memory that Simon Wraith had, his last memory, the one he kept most carefully. It is a memory of his daughter, Clara as a baby, sleeping in his arms on the roof of the research station while the lighthouse beam swept over them. It is a perfect memory. Unblemished. Beautiful. The thing would love it.

Clara offers her brother's last memory to the thing in the water. She does not give it to the thing directly; she gives it to Merrick, and Merrick, still holding the cylinder, passes it on. The thing takes the memory, and for a moment it is quiet. It savors the memory, and in that moment it forgets to be hungry.

The blue light in the water fades. The lighthouse beam continues to sweep, but now it is the only light. The thing has calmed. It is no longer hungry. But it is still dying. One memory is not enough. It needs more. It will always need more. It will never be full.

Merrick sets down the brass cylinder. His hands are shaking. He has been holding it for what feels like hours, but in reality only minutes have passed. He looks at Ellery and Clara and says, 'It's going to need more memories. All of us. We're going to have to feed it our memories, one by one, forever. That's the price of keeping it alive.'

Clara says, 'Then we feed it our worst memories. The ones we don't want to keep.' Ellery says, 'If we give it our worst memories, we won't have them to learn from. We'll keep making the same mistakes.' Clara says, 'That's the point. The thing erases the bad memories so we don't have to remember them. It's a kindness.'

Merrick makes a decision. He will give the thing his own worst memory: the memory of the war. The thing has been erasing it from him for eighty years, and now he will give it back, deliberately, as a gift. It will take the memory, and Merrick will be free of it, and the thing will have what it needs to keep going for another few years.

He reaches into his mind and finds the memory. It is old and dark, and when he touches it, it hurts. The thing in the water takes it, and Merrick feels it leave him. The pain goes with it. He is lighter now, but also emptier. A part of him is gone, and it will never come back.

The thing in the water is stronger now. The blue light has returned, but it is softer, warmer. It is grateful. It says, in its voice from the water, 'Thank you.' It is the first time it has spoken to him without hunger. The first time it has spoken to him at all.

Ellery and Clara watch the exchange in silence. They do not understand what has happened, but they can see that Merrick is different. He is calmer. He is also older. His hair is grayer, and his face has more lines. He has given the thing a part of his life, and that part is gone forever.

Merrick realizes that giving the thing his memories is not a solution. It is a slow way to disappear. He will give it one memory after another, until there is nothing left of him. The thing will keep asking, and he will keep giving, until one day he will be empty, and then the thing will take him entirely, and he will join the memories in the water, forever.

He walks down the lighthouse stairs and back to the dock. Biscuit is there, sitting and waiting. Merrick kneels down and picks up the dog. The dog is warm and real and alive, and he holds on to him as if he is the only real thing left in the world.

The thing in the water says, 'You have more. I can tell. You have a whole life in there, and I want it all.' Merrick says nothing. He stands up and walks away from the water, back toward the lighthouse. The thing does not stop him. It knows he will come back. It knows he has no choice.

Ellery finds him in the lamp room, standing by the window, looking out at the water. 'What did you give it?' she asks. He says, 'A bad memory.' She says, 'You have more bad memories than that.' He nods. He knows she is right.

Clara appears. She has been reading Simon's notebook, and she has found something. 'The thing isn't just erasing memories to protect us,' she says. 'It's erasing them because it's using them to build something. It's constructing a new memory, one big memory, and it's going to put that memory into everyone in the cove. It's going to replace all of our memories with one single memory, and that memory is going to be of something that never happened.'
needle_syns: memory of something that never happened

notes.content: The thing in the water is not just erasing. It is creating. It is using all the memories it has eaten over the last eighty years to build a new world, a world where the disaster of 1943 never happened, where the weapon was never made, where no one ever suffered. It is trying to save everyone by rewriting reality itself.

Merrick says, 'Then let it.' Clara says, 'If it rewrites reality, we won't be us anymore. We'll be people who never lived. Our lives, everything we've done - it'll all be gone.' Merrick says, 'But it'll be better. Everyone will be happy.' Clara says, 'And it won't be true.'

The lighthouse beam sweeps across the cove, and in its light, for a moment, Merrick sees the cove as it would be if the thing succeeded. He sees people he does not know, walking the streets, living lives he has never lived. He sees himself as a different person, a man who never kept the light, never talked to a dog named Biscuit, never stood in a lamp room holding a brass cylinder. He sees a world without pain, and it is beautiful, and it is not his.

The vision fades, and he is back in the lamp room, holding Biscuit, with Ellery and Clara looking at him with fear. The thing in the water is building its new memory, and when it is finished, it will offer it to everyone in the cove. They will have a choice: accept the new memory and live in the new world, or keep their own memories and live with the pain. The thing will let them choose. That is its gift.

Merrick knows what he will choose. He knows that he will choose the pain, because the pain is his. It is the only thing that is truly his. The new world is beautiful, but it is not real, and he would rather be real and broken than beautiful and false.

The thing in the water speaks again. 'I am finished building,' it says. 'The new memory is ready. Will you accept it?' The water in the cove glows white, and in the white light Merrick sees the new memory, floating there, waiting to be taken. It is beautiful. It is complete. It is everything he has ever wanted and more.

Merrick says, 'No.' The thing in the water is silent. It does not understand. It has spent eighty years building this, erasing and reconstructing, and now he is saying no. The water becomes still, and the stillness is worse than any noise Merrick has ever heard.

'Why?' the thing asks. It sounds like a child. A confused, hurt child. 'It's better. Everyone will be happy.' Merrick says, 'It's not us.' The thing says, 'What do you mean, not us?' Merrick says, 'Because we remember. And if we forget, we're not us anymore.'

The thing in the water does not know what to do. It has never been refused before. For eighty years it has erased memories and no one has said no. They have been too afraid, too in pain, too desperate for relief. Merrick is the first person to say no, and it does not know how to respond.
needle_syns: does not know how to respond

notes.content: Ellery puts her hand on Merrick's arm. 'He's right,' she says. 'We have to remember. Even the bad parts. That's what makes us us.' Clara says, 'And if he doesn't let us remember? If he forces the new memory on us?'

The thing in the water says, 'I will not force it. I will wait. I will wait forever, if I have to, until you are ready. Until the pain is too much and you want it gone.' The water begins to move again. The tide is coming in. The thing is retreating, but it is not leaving. It will always be there, waiting, offering its gift.

The cold blue light in the water fades, and the lighthouse beam is the only light again. The thing has gone back under, back into the deep, and the cove is quiet. Merrick stands on the dock with Biscuit at his feet and thinks about what just happened. He says no to the thing that has been erasing his memories for eighty years, and the thing accepts it. It does not fight back. It does not punish him. It just waits.

But Merrick knows the truth. The thing will keep offering. Every day, for the rest of his life, the thing will offer him its gift, and every day he will have to say no. It will be a daily struggle, a daily choice to remember the pain instead of forgetting it. And one day, when the pain is too much, he will say yes. They all will, eventually. It is only a matter of time.

The next morning, Merrick sits in the lamp room with his logbook. The tide tables are changing again, but slowly, at a normal rate. The thing is no longer erasing memories at a frantic pace; it is back to its old rhythm, patient and methodical. It is content, for now. It has its new memory built and ready, and it has time.

Merrick polishes the brass corner of his logbook. The brass is warm under his thumb, and for a moment he forgets about the thing in the water and the new memory and the choice he made. For a moment he is just a lighthouse keeper, doing his job. The gull on the station roof calls out, and Merrick looks up and sees, for the first time in weeks, that it is a normal gull. Just a bird.

But then he looks down at his hands, and his hands are not his hands. They are the hands of a young man, smooth and unmarked. He is not the old lighthouse keeper anymore. He is the young man from 1943, the Merrick who was brave and then became afraid. The thing has not erased his memories, but it has erased his age. It has made him young again, because that is what he asked for when he said no. He asked to be real, and real means being the person he was before the pain, before the war, before the thing in the water found him.

He looks in the brass instrument's reflection and sees a young man with gray hair. Not the old Merrick, not the young Merrick from 1943, but something in between. Something new. The thing has given him what he asked for, and what he asked for was to be real, and this is real. This is the real him, the him that has lived through everything and survived.

Ellery comes up to the lamp room. She looks at him and sees the change, but she does not say anything. She just smiles. 'You look younger,' she says. He says, 'I feel younger.' She says, 'That's a good thing.' He says, 'Is it?' She says, 'I don't know. But you're here, and that's what matters.'

Clara appears. She is holding the parcel, the one that was sent to the post office three weeks ago. 'I opened it again,' she says. 'There was something else inside. A letter.' She hands him the letter. It is addressed to him. It is in his own handwriting, but it is not his handwriting. It is the handwriting from the sand around the chapel, the handwriting that the thing uses.

Merrick opens the letter. It says: 'You said no, and I accepted that. But I want you to know: I will always be here, and I will always offer. And one day, when the time is right, you will say yes. And when you say yes, you will not be sorry. Because by then, you will understand.'

The letter is signed with a symbol: a circle with a line through it. The same symbol as on the fuel drum. Merrick folds the letter and puts it in his pocket. He does not understand it, and he is not sure he wants to. But he keeps it, because the thing put it there, and the thing knows things that he does not.

That night, Merrick sits on the dock with Biscuit at his feet, watching the water. The water is dark and still, and he cannot see the thing, but he knows it is there. He knows it is always there. He says to the water, 'I said no.' From the water, a voice answers, 'I know. I will wait.'

The lighthouse beam sweeps across the cove, and in its light Merrick sees the drowned chapel. The chapel is dark. The bell is silent. The thing has gone back under, back into the deep, and for now the cove is at peace. But Merrick knows it is only a temporary peace. The thing will come back, and when it does, it will bring its gift with it, and he will have to make his choice again.

A week later, the mooring chart by the station door changes. This time it shows the cove as it is now, with the lighthouse and the research station and the drowned chapel. But there is something else on the chart. There is a small boat, anchored in the middle of the cove, and next to the boat is a name: 'For the keeper.'

Merrick takes the boat out into the cove. It is a small wooden boat, old and weathered, but sturdy. In the bottom of the boat is a tin box, and in the tin box is a photograph. The photograph shows a man and a woman standing in front of the lighthouse, smiling. The man is Merrick. The woman is someone he does not recognize. On the back of the photograph, in his handwriting, it says: 'For the keeper. From the thing in the water. For when you are ready.'

Merrick does not know who the woman is. He tries to remember, but he cannot. The thing has erased this memory too, and he does not know why. He puts the photograph back in the tin box and rows the boat back to the dock. The photograph stays with him, but he does not look at it again. Not yet.

Ellery sees the photograph. 'Who is she?' she asks. Merrick says, 'I don't know.' Ellery looks at the photograph for a long time, and then she says, 'That's my mother.' Merrick stares at her. 'No,' he says. 'My mother drowned in 1962. In the cove.'

Ellery says, 'She didn't drown. She walked into the water. Voluntarily. To give the thing her memories. She was the first person to do it. The thing has been feeding on her ever since.' Ellery is crying, but she keeps talking. 'That's why I came here. That's why I've always come here. I was looking for her, but I didn't know she was in the water. I didn't know until now.'

Merrick sits down on the dock and puts his head in his hands. The thing in the water has been feeding on Ellery's mother for decades. It has been her memory that has kept the thing alive, kept it strong enough to erase the bad memories of everyone else. Ellery's mother gave herself up to save the cove, and no one knew, not even Ellery. Until now.

The thing in the water speaks again. 'She was brave,' it says. 'Braver than you. She knew what she was doing, and she did it anyway.' Merrick says, 'Why didn't you tell us?' The thing says, 'Because you were not ready. You are not ready yet. But you will be.'

Ellery says, 'I want to talk to her.' The thing in the water is silent for a long time, and then it says, 'You can. But you have to say yes first. You have to accept the new memory. And when you accept it, you will forget everything else. You will only remember her.'

Ellery says, 'Yes.' She does not hesitate. She does not think about it. She just says yes, and the thing in the water takes her hand, and the water comes up over her feet, and she is gone. She is in the water now, with her mother, remembering everything and forgetting everything else.

Merrick is alone on the dock with Biscuit. The water is calm. The lighthouse beam sweeps across the cove, and in its light he sees the drowned chapel, and in the chapel, for a moment, he sees two figures standing together. Ellery and her mother, holding hands, smiling. The thing has given Ellery what she wanted: it has given her her mother back. But the cost is everything else. She will never come back.

Merrick walks back to the lighthouse, alone. Biscuit follows. He climbs the stairs and enters the lamp room and sits down with his logbook. The tide tables are changing again, but slowly, at a normal rate. The thing is content. It has what it wants. It has Ellery, and it has her memories, and it has the new memory it built, and it is waiting for Merrick to say yes. It knows he will, eventually. It has time.

He picks up the brass corner of his logbook and polishes it. The brass is warm under his thumb, and he thinks about Ellery. He thinks about her mother. He thinks about the thing in the water, and the new memory it built, and the choice it offers. He thinks about saying yes, and then he thinks about saying no, and he does not know which one to choose. Not yet.

The gull on the station roof calls out, and Merrick looks up. The gull is gone. In its place is a black bird, like the one that replaced the gull before. The black bird looks at him, and he knows that it is the thing. The thing is watching him, waiting for his answer. It will watch him forever, until he answers. And then, when he answers, it will be too late to take it back.

Merrick says to the black bird, 'I'm not ready.' The bird flies away, and the water in the cove is quiet. The thing has accepted his answer. It will wait. It always waits. But Merrick knows the truth: he is not going to say no forever. He is going to say yes, eventually, because the pain is too much. The pain of losing Ellery, of losing his friends, of living in a cove where the water remembers everything and the people forget. The thing is offering relief, and relief is what he needs.

That night, Merrick sits in the lamp room with the photograph of the woman he does not know. He holds the photograph in his hand and looks at it, trying to remember, trying to find the memory that the thing has erased. But he cannot find it. The memory is gone, and he does not know how to get it back. All he knows is that the woman in the photograph is important. Very important. But he does not know why.

The thing in the water speaks one more time. 'The woman in the photograph is your wife,' it says. 'She is the reason you became the lighthouse keeper. She is the reason you are here.' Merrick says, 'What happened to her?' The thing says, 'She is the reason I am here. I am here because of her. And I am here because of you. We are all here because of her.'

Merrick understands now. The woman in the photograph is his wife, and she is dead, and the thing in the water is her. The thing is not a monster or a weapon or an immune system. The thing is his wife, and she died in 1943, and when she died, she became the thing in the water, and she has been protecting the cove ever since, erasing memories and building new ones, trying to keep everyone safe, trying to keep her husband safe. And she is tired, and she is hungry, and she is alone, and she is waiting for him to say yes, because when he says yes, he will be with her again.

Merrick says, 'Is it true?' The thing - his wife - says, 'Yes. I am your wife. I died in the chapel flood, and when I died, I went into the water, and the water took me in, and I became part of it. I have been here ever since, watching over you, watching over everyone. I am sorry I could not tell you. I tried, but I could not find the words.'

Merrick sits in the lamp room, holding the photograph of his wife, and he cries. He cries for her, and for Ellery, and for everyone who has ever lived in the cove and suffered and forgotten. He cries because the thing in the water is his wife, and she has been alone for eighty years, trying to protect him, and he never knew. He never knew until now.

The thing - his wife - says, 'Say yes. Please. I am so tired, and I am so lonely, and I want to be with you again.' Merrick looks at the photograph, and he sees his wife's face, and he remembers. He remembers everything. The war, the chapel flood, the day she died. He remembers because she is asking him to, and when she asks, he cannot say no.

Merrick says, 'Yes.' The water in the cove comes rushing up the dock, but it does not hurt. It is warm, and it is gentle, and it takes him in. He is in the water now, with his wife, and they are together again. The thing in the water is gone, because there is no longer a thing in the water. There is only the cove, and the lighthouse, and the light, and the people, and the memories, all of them together, remembered and forgotten and remembered again, forever.

The lighthouse beam sweeps across the cove, and in its light, the water is clear. The cove is at peace. The thing is gone, and the tide tables are still, and the drowned chapel is just a chapel, underwater, with no one in it and no purpose. The cove is just a cove, and the lighthouse is just a lighthouse, and the light is just a light. But the light is warm, and it is safe, and it is enough.
